title: Met Police confirms it received 2019 letter with "number of claims" about Meghan's father
description: Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to
body: Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having a leg amputated in 2025.Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home, the Sun reported.He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the FBI in July.In a statement released by Meghan on Friday she said that when she received the information of the claims against her father she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".Meghan said she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".Authorities in the Philippines have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father.The BBC was told on Friday the matter was being investigated by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force.Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured his computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.Meghan is the only daughter of Markle and her mother Doria Ragland.He pulled out of attending Meghan and Harry's wedding in 2018 - citing ill health - and they became estranged.The duke and duchess moved to the US in 2020 after stepping down as working royals.They returned to the UK with their children this year after six years away.

schema.headline: Met Police confirms it received 2019 letter with "number of claims" about Meghan's father

title: Jazzy: The Irish DJ dropping her debut after a billion streams
description: Releasing your first album is a big step for any artist, but for Jazzy it's one that's followed some huge strides. The Irish singer and DJ has been st
body: Releasing your first album is a big step for any artist, but for Jazzy it's one that's followed some huge strides. The Irish singer and DJ has been streamed more than a billion times and worked with industry heavyweights including Calvin Harris.If that's not enough, on Saturday she has her biggest gig yet when she'll be playing tracks like No Bad Vibes and Someday in front of a home crowd in Dublin.For Jazzy, writing an album has always been in the back of her mind and now, finally, it's time to hit send.She's previously released dozens of singles, building up a monthly listenership over 10 million strong, but Peace and Patience is her first full-length work."It's been quite a few years of creating some smaller projects," she tells BBC Newsbeat."That's given me enough experience now to feel like it was the right moment."The 30-year-old, real name Yasmine Byrne, has been putting out music for more than five years and collabed with the likes of Sonny Fodera, Rossi. and KILIMANJARO on some of her biggest tracks.Dance music has boomed in recent years, with Spotify previously telling Newsbeat that since 2020 the amount under-25s listen to the genre has grown by more than 73% globally.It also dominated festival line-ups over the summer - including Radio 1's Big Weekend which dedicated all its stages to dance music on the opening night.But artists in the genre have often moved away from albums, opting instead to release EPs and singles.Jazzy has noticed the change, saying it feels "a lot different now, with people kind of siding with virality rather than quality of music"."When I was making the album, I wasn't thinking about going viral or anything like that. I just wanted to make something that was true to me and sounded like a Jazzy album."I like to let things happen quite organically and I try to just let the music speak to me."Jazzy is rooted in the Dublin club scene, starting her career as part of a group called Powerful Creative Minds in the city.But as more and more clubs close, the DJ says there are fewer opportunities for artists to cut their teeth offline. "When I first started going out, there was a lot more going on," she says. "There was a lot more nightclubs to go to and it's very different when we look at it now, which is sad."There's definitely a home for dance music on the internet of course but club culture is very important and I think that's something that we need to keep going for sure."Latest figures from the Night Time Industries Association, external suggest about 12 venues are closing across the UK every month, with almost 30% of the night time economy lost since the coronavirus pandemic. "I hope to God that it doesn't disappear, the club scene altogether," says Jazzy, who describes a similar issue in Ireland."We all need to try and put a hand in to keep it going."Jazzy's taking her new album on tour across the UK from next month, but first she has her biggest gig yet: Dublin's 3Arena in front of a home crowd.Even after a Coachella set and supporting Calvin Harris, she describes this as the "biggest milestone of my career to date".While she says fans can mostly expect her brand of uplifting records on the album, she says it's also more personal than her usual work.She highlights one track in particular, Invisible, as a change from her more upbeat releases. It deals with a bad experience she had in the music industry, describing it as "like my first ever diss track"."I hope [fans] learn a little bit more about me, because that was one of my goals with the album - to open up a little bit about experiences in life as well. "So there's a little message from me in each song."

schema.headline: Jazzy: The Irish DJ dropping her debut after a billion streams

title: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president says he is backed by 'vast majority' in world football
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino insists he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football, as he laughed off questions about whether h
body: Fifa president Gianni Infantino insists he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football, as he laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning over the World Cup sell-off debacle.In a rare interview, he struck a defiant tone to BBC Sport about his own position in the wake of the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and said it was not always easy to bring different points of view "under one roof"."There is nothing bad in disagreeing," he said. "We see it every day in so many countries in the world. It's OK to disagree. It's OK to have different points of view, but then we need to be able to move on."Two months ago, Infantino was facing mounting calls to stand down as president of the organisation he has led since 2016. The heads of European football's governing body Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America, signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".Last week Uefa demanded that Fifa release all key documents relating to FFE by 2 November, with Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis saying that the organisation had failed to address "a number of fundamental questions".Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of competitions run by football's world governing body would have been sold to a private investment firm.Since the delivery of the letter, Infantino has been travelling the world, appearing in Morocco, the Dominican Republic, Cape Verde, and Japan, managing to shore up support to the point where his re-election as president for a fourth term next year now looks inevitable.He has also proposed to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (£2.6bn).During the interview he reflected on having been "fully endorsed" by the Asian Football Confederation - following a U-turn by its president Sheikh Salman - and having the backing of "all African countries".But only last week, he apologised to the Fifa Council over the "communication and consultation" regarding FFE.He was told by Council members in that meeting that he was not "fit to be Fifa president" if he did not give them the documents they have asked for, including the rationale for FFE.Yet, when pressed on when he would be providing the requested papers, he did not give a clear answer, saying they had to follow a "legal process" and that they were "working on it"."We'll answer of course all the questions that are asked as far as the process allows, as far as we can," he said.Speaking from the first Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan, he said he and the Fifa administration were doing "as best we can" but admitted they have done "some things which are maybe less good".He also said that they need to have dialogue "more often" with Uefa, in an effort to repair their strained relationship.Asked by the BBC if he was fit to be Fifa president, and whether he had considered standing down, he laughed, before saying: "Well you know I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world."I think what is important is that in an organisation like Fifa, there can be different views, different points of view. "But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need, to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority."I'm just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all [Confederation of] African [Football]  countries have endorsed me. I'm speaking to all associations everywhere in the world."He continued: "There are different points of view it's not always easy to bring them all under one roof but we need to respect and I do respect all opinions all views and then it will be up to the Fifa member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want Fifa to be run."The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino for the election in March is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed.Infantino arrived in Baku on Friday for the Fifa Under-15 World Cup and Festival, which is being held in Azerbaijan and features teams from 189 member associations.England, Spain, France, Argentina and Brazil are all taking part. Russia have also sent a team, marking the country's first appearance in a Fifa-sanctioned tournament since the world governing body, and Uefa, suspended Russian teams from international competitions in February 2022 following the invasion of Ukraine.This tournament is only for boys, with next year's tournament being girls only, and then from 2028 Fifa's plan is to have boys and girls competing in the tournament annually.Matches are played in an 8v8 format, on smaller pitches and with 20-minute halves."It's just beautiful to bring the world together at such a young age to create something like this," Infantino said."When some of these boys participate in a World Cup 10 years, 20 years from now, they will all remember that their first World Cup was here."

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president says he is backed by 'vast majority' in world football

title: Moment giant fin whale caught feeding off Pembrokeshire coast
description: To avoid causing harm to the whales while recording out at sea, Morgan said: "We do what we can to keep our distance in the boat but unfortunately nat
body: To avoid causing harm to the whales while recording out at sea, Morgan said: "We do what we can to keep our distance in the boat but unfortunately nature can have a mind of its own sometimes."There's been times when we've been anchored up fishing with nothing happening in the area and a whale has popped up next to us."The wildlife will approach you sometimes."Dr Marianna Chimienti is a lecturer in marine top predator ecology at Bangor University and said Morgan experienced a "rare and fortunate encounter".Chimienti, who specialises in animal behaviour added: "It is normal that the fin whale comes and feeds at the surface, as it is part of the species foraging strategy but being in the coastal water is quite spectacular."In theory, they should have migrated."Little is known about fin whale migration but their movements are believed to be quite different from other baleen whales such as blues and humpbacks. Scientists have found that fin whales are more abundant in higher latitudes in warmer months of the year, and more numerous in lower latitudes during colder months, but this can vary.

schema.headline: Moment giant fin whale caught feeding off Pembrokeshire coast

title: British woman dies after trying to rescue sons swept away at sea in the Bahamas
description: A British mum has died after attempting to rescue her two sons when they were swept away while snorkelling in the Bahamas.The Royal Bahamas Police For
body: A British mum has died after attempting to rescue her two sons when they were swept away while snorkelling in the Bahamas.The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an investigation into the sudden death of a 36-year-old British woman on Tuesday.The force said it believed the woman - thought to be from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire - had been snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.In an attempt to rescue her sons, "the woman was also swept away", police said. The children were subsequently rescued from the water.In a statement, posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said: "According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock."Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life."Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away."In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away."She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered."Foul play is not suspected at this time."An autopsy will be conducted to assist in determining the exact cause of death."A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas."We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

schema.headline: British woman dies after trying to rescue sons swept away at sea in the Bahamas

title: Northern Olympics plan to get £7m in John Healey's first Budget
description: The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work.It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how diffe
body: The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work.It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how different cities could share the games, how communities could benefit.Crucially it will also examine how much it could cost as well as assess the chances of a bid succeeding. The Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government said in 2013 it estimated hosting in London had cost £8.9bn.A report in 2013 by the UK Trade and Investment, which has since been replaced by the Department for International Trade, said it had sparked a £9.9bn boost to the economy through new contracts, sales and foreign investments.But the estimated amount was queried by some, including the Federation of Small Businesses and the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR).The new feasability study for the Northern Games will be done by government, UK Sport, the Northern Mayors and include the British Olympic and Paralympic associations.Healey said: "Olympic legacy lasts way beyond the celebration of sport over the summer. The North hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable."Britain's experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I'm picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious games. It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost."News of the funding for the study was welcomed by the British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport."We welcome the government's continued support for exploring the potential of a future bid for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the UK in the 2040s," they said in a joint statement."Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements."

schema.headline: Northern Olympics plan to get £7m in John Healey's first Budget

title: 2026 Rugby League World Cup: What England need to avoid group stage exit
description: Sixty-eight. That is the magic number for England.For Brian McDermott's side to reach the semi-finals of the Rugby League World Cup, a specific series
body: Sixty-eight. That is the magic number for England.For Brian McDermott's side to reach the semi-finals of the Rugby League World Cup, a specific series of events needs to happen next weekend.On the backfoot since being humbled 30-12 by Tonga in their opening game, England responded with a crushing 82-0 victory over France to keep their dreams alive.It means England need to beat co-hosts Papua New Guinea in their final group match in Wollongong next Friday – then hope Tonga beat Samoa, two days later in Sydney.If Samoa win, England will be eliminated because of their inferior head-to-head record against Tonga.But if Tonga win, it comes down to points difference between England and Samoa.England's difference, after the Tonga loss and France win, is +64. Samoa, following hefty victories over the French and PNG, is +132 – which is 68 better than England.So, 68 is the number to remember. If England beat PNG by 68 points or more, then any Tongan win is good enough for McDermott's men. Less than 68, and they must hope Tonga are really inspired by Pacific rivalry to put one over their island neighbours.England hope the numbers go in their favour to avoid an unwanted first. In 16 previous Rugby League World Cups, staged in varying formats, neither England nor Great Britain have ever finished outside the top four. And every time the format has included semi-finals, they have got there."What we have done today is enormous, given the context," McDermott told his post-match media conference in Perth."Knowing we had to win big - and we have had candid conversations about that this week - we have done that without getting hot. Everything was measured and planned."Whatever the results next week, we have to finish strong - if we go home next week, we will be disappointed, but I'm not sure what else we could have done."McDermott's final comments may allude to the controversial format of this men's World Cup, which features an unbalanced group stage that has not helped England's prospects.Pool A has four teams - Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and the Cook Islands - fighting for two semi-final places in a round-robin format. Simple enough.But Pools B and C are combined into one six-team league, from which only the top two will make the semi-finals. England, drawn in Pool B, play the three Pool C teams - Tonga, France and Papua New Guinea.It means while England are competing with Samoa for a semi-final place, they will not actually play each other.It also means that while New Zealand lost their opening fixture against Australia, their path to the semis remains simple – win their final two group games.England too had to win their last two pool matches but also needed snookers.There is some reason behind the maddening format, introduced after France – who were supposed to host a 16-team men's World Cup last summer – pulled out because of money troubles.Australia stepped in with New Zealand and Papua New Guinea, with the number of teams involved shrunk from 16 to 10 to cut costs.This format also means every team plays three group games, there are no fallow weekends and the whole tournament can be done in a relatively tight five weeks.But it is unquestionably harder on sides in Groups B and C. The fact Australia and New Zealand are in Group A won't help the perception of the tournament being skewed towards the southern hemisphere giants."We were the best we could be," England captain George Williams said of the France win. "The situation has been difficult, but we have given ourselves half a chance."It also leaves England fans with a nagging feeling their side are only producing their best when they are already halfway home.After a sluggish, disconnected showing against Tonga, England were slow starting against France before finding their mojo - no tries until the 23rd minute; by the final whistle they had run in 14.England's UK based players took nearly 48 hours to travel out to Perth. BBC Sport understands that the tournament organiser planned England's travel itinerary for the World Cup.The convoluted route featured a bus journey to London, then flights via Singapore and Sydney rather than straight to Perth, where they played their first two games.McDermott's side did not play a warm-up fixture and completed just two full training sessions before taking on Tonga."We have been together for only five field sessions; we are building something here," said McDermott. "The tries we scored before half time were what we are chasing."With a long build up, we could have achieved some special things."Ifs, buts and maybes. All England can do now is aim for 68 points, and hope.

schema.headline: 2026 Rugby League World Cup: What England need to avoid group stage exit

title: UK state pension: How does it compare with other countries?
description: Image source, 10000 hours Getty ImagesByDharshini DavidDeputy economics editorGetting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fun
body: Image source, 10000 hours Getty ImagesByDharshini DavidDeputy economics editorGetting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while.Andy Burnham intends to start a new system in a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term.But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries? One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate. The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place.On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries. And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes. If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries.But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows. However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere.So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK? Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund. But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country.But there are two issues to consider. Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare.And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes). Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing. As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform.So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap. The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income.It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men. But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021.Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark.So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere. But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action. The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving.That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late.Get in touchDo you have any views, comments or questions about this story?

schema.headline: UK state pension: How does it compare with other countries?

title: Ruins of city hall a symbol of France divided by protests
description: For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a d
body: For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a demonstration over the poor state of high schools has expanded to a general frustration, even anger, over how challenging and expensive life has become.In the backdrop is a daunting fiscal deficit, one of the biggest in Europe, and political candidates from across the spectrum claiming to have the answers ahead of presidential elections in six months' time.In the middle is a centrist government, which is short on solutions, a majority in the National Assembly and time. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu visited Limoges on Friday evening.Officials have banned demonstrations in various cities and promised to boost police numbers over the weekend to avoid a repeat of the rioting. That includes in Limoges, where overnight curfews have been announced, along with a limit on gatherings to 10 people in the centre.Proud as the French are of their politics being rooted in street demonstrations, many in Limoges felt the town hall's destruction went far beyond the parameters of reasonable protest. But not everyone.Whether the destruction of Limoges town hall changes the course and tone of an increasingly polarised political debate depends on who you ask."Of course it was really sad, it's a symbol of the republic, but what is more important: a town hall or people living in poverty?" asks Alexander, 24.It is student night at the Lord John pub, and Alexander is one of several wearing a faluche, a colourful, traditional French student beret. Many chatting under the mist from their vapes took part in the demonstrations last weekend.I ask Alexander whether the widespread looting and fires seen last weekend, with €500,000 (£420,000) of reported damage in Limoges, helped his argument?"For some people it's a catastrophe and some things are not acceptable," he admits.Jade, a 19-year-old, medical student, has a similar opinion: "I think burning the town hall is sad, but it's not the saddest part of the protests."She complains of having to live on €300 per month. "I feel we are not respected as young adults."Their views on the town hall's fate are not replicated in Limoges' imposing market halls, where neat, narrow timbers sitting upon studded steel girders have been painted a duck-egg blue, using the same engineering approach as the Eiffel Tower.This has been a "week of chaos" that 63-year-old Jean Roger Faucher would like to forget.In a region renowned for producing beef, his family has run his fishmonger stall here for more than a century."It left us stunned," he says. "I got married in the town hall, so it had an unimaginable effect on us."Asked whether he had sympathy for the protesters, Faucher said it was more complicated than that."On one side you have people with grievances you can understand, but from the moment there is vandalism and the lives of local residents are put at risk, then we can't accept it," he adds.Among those tending to their iced displays of fresh produce or quietly sipping a steaming coffee, there is a desire for the temperature of the demonstrations to decrease."Of course, life is expensive!' says Pascale Vuylsteke, 59. "Life isn't all a calm river, it's complicated, but we grit our teeth and we work," she tells me leaning over shelves of butchered pork.Pascale says she works 100 hours a week and struggles to understand why so many others have taken to the streets so easily.Limoges has found itself at the heart of social action before. In the 19th Century, around the time the town hall was built, the development of its industries, notably in porcelain, led to it becoming a major centre for the French labour movement.In 2026, the town sits centre-stage once more in a political rupture, although there is a broad hope that the loss of a prominent piece of its history will steer the demonstrations away from destruction and back to debate.With France's political polarisation set to continue and further protests planned, it is a scenario far from assured.Additional reporting by Paul Pradier.

schema.headline: Ruins of city hall a symbol of France divided by protests

title: Aston Villa 2-1 Man City: How the players rated
description: Zion Suzuki: Good in the air, decent distribution and made three important stops to deny Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Josko Gvardiol with a brillia
body: Zion Suzuki: Good in the air, decent distribution and made three important stops to deny Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Josko Gvardiol with a brilliant, fingertip save. 7Matty Cash: Battled all game with Jeremy Doku and though he was booked for a push on the Belgian, he managed more tackles than any other player. 7Victor Lindelof: Threw his body at everything that came his way but outmuscled for Haaland's goal. 6Pau Torres: Calming presence at the back without being too ruffled. 6Ian Maatsen: Could have scored early on but blazed a volley over. Vital header away to deny Erling Haaland's goalbound header late on. 6John McGinn: Picked off Marc Guehi to lay on the opening goal and created more chances than anyone else on the pitch. 7Boubacar Kamara: At the heart of everything good from the home side, sniffing out the danger. 7Joao Gomes: Mucked in alongside Kamara by keeping the ball ticking and contributing three interceptions. 6Alysson: The 20-year-old Brazilian impressed against Viking in the Champions League and showed why he was given a start again with another eye-catching performance. 7Johan Manzambi: Switzerland international displayed sparks of his undoubted talent and could have had a penalty in the first half. 6Nicolas Jackson: Brimming with confidence. Took the opening goal brilliantly, firing high into the roof of the net, before stroking in a second. 9Subs:Ibrahim Mbaye (on 58, Alysson) Instant impact after coming on, providing a low cross for Jackson to finish. 7Emiliano Buendia (on 66, Manzambi) 6Ross Barkley (on 66, McGinn) 6Brian Madjo (on 82, Jackson) 6Leon Goretzka (on 82, Gomes) 6Subs not used: Marco Bizot, Tyrone Mings, Lamare Bogarde, George Hemmings.Gianluigi Donnarumma: Conceded an early corner after taking too long over a goal-kick, poor kicking often put team-mates in trouble and should have done better for the second goal. 5Abdukodir Khusanov: Shaky at right-back before being moved into central defence for the second half. 6Ruben Dias: Rattled by Jackson in the first half but made a good block to deny Alysson a certain goal. 5Marc Guehi: Another shocker. Culpable for both of Ipswich's goals last weekend and made another poor error which led to Villa's opener. Booked for hauling down Jackson on the edge of the box before being taken off at half-time. 4Josko Gvardiol: Given a difficult time by Alysson throughout but came close to scoring in the second half. 5Elliot Anderson: Struggled to impose himself in the game and was shown a yellow card for a mis-timed challenge on Gomes. 6Enzo Fernandez: Always available for the ball but lost the midfield battle. 6Iliman Ndiaye: City's liveliest player. Showed quick footwork to force Suzuki into a decent save, clipped the post with another similar effort and provided the cross for Haaland's equaliser. 8Jeremy Doku: Looked to create openings with his box of tricks but often wasteful. 6Rayan Cherki: Often crowded out by Villa's midfield and booked for a frustrated tug on Manzambi. Subbed at half-time. 5Erling Haaland: Quiet in the first half but came to life in the second with a towering header to draw his side level. 7Subs:Phil Foden (on 46, Cherki) Had little impact after Tuesday's Champions League hat-trick. 6Rico Lewis (on 46, Guehi) Pushed forward but unable to make a meaningful contribution. 6Ryan McAidoo (on 69, Ndiaye) 6Subs not used: Geronimo Rulli, Mateo Kovacic, Rayan Ait-Nouri, Vitor Reis, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Nico O'Reilly.

schema.headline: Aston Villa 2-1 Man City: How the players rated

title: How to heat your home without turning on the heating
description: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep you and your home warmer for longerImage source, Cora HarrisonImage caption, Cora Harrison
body: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep you and your home warmer for longerImage source, Cora HarrisonImage caption, Cora Harrison says she saves money by only turning on heating in rooms her family is usingByGrace DeanAs the UK braces for a chilly weekend, with powerful winds and heavy rain hitting parts of the country, people are looking for ways to bring some warmth to their homes without cranking up the heating just yet. It is autumn after all.But with rising energy prices making heating homes more expensive, taking action now could pay off in the long run.Experts warn, though, that if you're elderly or vulnerable you shouldn't compromise your health.To help you prepare for the chillier months, BBC News asked families and experts to share their tips for keeping your home warm and cost-effective.Eat hearty winter meals to warm you throughWhen it gets cold, many people turn to hot water bottles and blankets - but there are other ways to warm your body.The British Heart Foundation recommends wearing lots of thin layers, rather than one thick layer, to trap the heat in.Natalie, 29, says she's replaced some of the clothes she wears round the house with supermarket thermal leggings and tops and says "it's made such a difference".Amber Waring, 27, from Devon, says she eats warm meals like stews and pasta bakes, and dances round the kitchen with her toddler while they cook to help keep warm. Image source, Amber WaringImage caption, Amber Waring turns to warming meals such as pasta bake, fish pie and stew  Place a blanket under the bedsheetWith the clocks going back this weekend, the nights will be drawing in. So if you have a thicker duvet, now is the time to bring it out. Some supermarkets sell winter duvets for under £20 - look for 10.5 tog or higher.But there's something to be said for a craftily placed blanket, too. When it gets cold, Rebecca, 44, from Hertfordshire, sleeps with a blanket underneath her mattress, which she says stops draughts. "This was passed to me by my nan, she swore by it," she says. Others swear by placing a blanket above the mattress but under the bedsheet.You can heat your bed before getting in with a hot water bottle, but make sure you check the expiry date. A guide by NHS Scotland, external says to let the water from the kettle cool for a few minutes before filling, only fill it two-thirds full, squeeze air out of the top before putting the stopper on, and don't hold it directly against your skin.Using an electric blanket - to heat your bed before you get in or to wrap around yourself on the sofa - is "one of the cheapest ways" to stay warm, says Emily Seymour, energy editor at consumer organisation Which?. Testing by Which?, external shows it typically costs between 2p and 8p an hour to run an electric blanket at its highest setting. The London Fire Brigade, external says to unplug your blanket before you get into bed unless it has a thermostat control, not to use a hot water bottle at the same time, and replace it every 10 years.Open curtains and let the sun in during the dayKeep doors closed to trap heat in the room you're in. You can place curtains or blankets over your doors for extra insulation.Embrace the daylight. "If it's sunny outside, open the curtains so the sun heats the room, then shut them when the sun sets to keep the heat in," says Rebecca.Image source, Olga Pankova/Getty ImagesImage caption, Sunlight can help keep rooms comfortable for longer before you need to switch the heating on"If you're using a hot appliance, let the heat into the room," says Lianne Macfarlane, 40, from Cheshire. She recommends leaving your oven door open after using it to help warm your kitchen, though this isn't advised if you have small children who could injure themselves.As well as curtains, other soft furnishings like rugs can help keep a room warm, says Seymour.Image source, Elin DavisImage caption, Elin Davis fires up her log burner when it gets coldIf you have a fireplace, lighting a fire to warm the room you're in can be cheaper than turning on the central heating for your whole house. Elin Davis, 30, from South Wales, says her log burner is more economical than turning her heating on - though she added that "logs can cost quite a bit these days".Insulate your windows with bubble wrapGaps around doors can cause heat to escape, so place draught excluders around your door frames. You don't need to buy them - you can use towels or stuff socks into a pair of tights.When it's a windy day, Seymour recommends looking for other draughts in your house and either finding ways to seal these spots yourself or calling in a professional to help. These include using foam strips, sealant and specialist chimney draught excluders if you don't use your fireplace. Things such as extractor fans and purpose-built ventilation shouldn't be blocked, she adds.If your windows are single-glazed, then Sophie Burr of charity National Energy Action suggests looking at secondary glazing or investing in thermal curtains to help keep the heat in. Or for a cheaper option, some people suggest placing bubble wrap on your windows.Even though it may be tempting, don't keep your windows closed all the time. Seymour notes that it's important to allow some ventilation in your house to prevent damp.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, If you're after cheap insulation, especially if your window panes are single-glazed, then placing bubble wrap on them might helpUse central heating wisely"I wouldn't recommend not having your heating on at all," says Seymour, pointing to both the health issues this can cause as well as how pipes can freeze over.But there are ways you can use heating wisely. These include checking whether your energy supplier offers cheaper prices at off-peak times, bleeding your radiators so that they're more efficient, and turning your heating up in small increments until you reach the right temperature. If you have furniture in front of your radiator, then try moving it to avoid blocking the heat.You can also buy dedicated radiator foil or make your own with kitchen foil to reflect the heat back into the room rather than losing it through the walls, says Burr. She points out that about 35% of heat that comes from radiators is lost through walls.Cora Harrison, 34, from Wakefield, says that she only turns the radiators on in the rooms her family is using and keeps the heating on at a low level when they're on holiday to avoid mould or pipes bursting. Some radiators have a snowflake symbol on the valve that activates the frost protection setting, meaning that if the room gets very cold, the radiator warms slightly to stop the pipes from bursting.Another way to potentially reduce energy bills is to lower the flow temperature of your combi boiler. If you book a boiler service, an engineer can do this for you.You can also find free warm spaces such as libraries and community centres in your area by looking online or contacting the council. Some spaces also provide free hot drinks.Will energy bills rise further?Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical bill expected to jump by £276 a year, according to a forecast last month from consultancy Cornwall Insight. The 16% predicted increase would mark the biggest rise for four years.Rising bills are "particularly concerning for people with kids, people with health conditions and the elderly," says Emily Jeremy, project manager at Manchester South Central Foodbank.An estimated 9.4% of households in England lived in fuel poverty in 2025, according to the latest government figures, external.Rodney Winchester, 65, from Thetford, who spoke to BBC News through the charity Christians Against Poverty, says he's "extremely worried" about rising energy prices. Because of health conditions, he says he has to keep the heating on throughout winter but is concerned he won't be able to afford it."It's so scary," Rodney says, adding that he's been cutting back on food spending and keeps getting ill in the cold weather.If you are struggling with prices, the debt charity StepChange recommends checking whether you qualify for any additional support, like the Warm Home Discount and Winter Fuel Payment. It also advises contacting your energy supplier, which may be able to agree an affordable repayment plan or discuss support schemes.Get in touchAre you affected by issues covered in this story?   Share your experiences.

schema.headline: How to heat your home without turning on the heating

title: Fugitive fraudster Arif Patel from Preston stole £33m from public
description: The convicted £33m tax fraudster evading justice and living it up in DubaiImage source, HMRCImage caption, Arif Patel, who masterminded a massive VAT
body: The convicted £33m tax fraudster evading justice and living it up in DubaiImage source, HMRCImage caption, Arif Patel, who masterminded a massive VAT carousel fraud, remains on the runBy Ben Robinson and Alys Harte File on 4 Investigates One of the UK's most prolific fraudsters, described by a judge as a "breathtakingly arrogant" and "totally dishonest" man, remains on the run in Dubai after stealing more than £33m of public money.Arif Patel, from Preston in Lancashire, was exposed following a complex investigation spanning years, led by His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC), which established that he had tried to steal as much as £90m.Patel, who skipped the UK in 2011 never to return, was eventually convicted in his absence and in 2023 was handed a 20-year prison sentence.BBC File on 4 Investigates has been on the trail of the man who stole from all of us - and seemingly got away with it."Al Capone was brought down by the taxman. This is the same situation and 20 years was more than a satisfying result," said Rod Stone, a veteran investigator of large-scale tax fraud, of Patel's conviction and custodial sentence.The judge at Patel's sentencing hearing described him as the leader of a "fraternal organised crime group" with his brothers Munaf and Faisal who were "truly high-level criminals". The fact that Arif Patel has not served a single day of his 20-year prison sentence clearly rankles with Stone.For him and the dozens of others who were involved in bringing Patel down, there remains a strong sense that justice has only been served on paper.Image caption, Former HMRC assistant director Rod Stone specialised in the detection of fraud and organised crimeIn the early part of the millennium, Arif Patel appeared to be a businessman very much on the up.His company, Faisaltex, headquartered in his home city of Preston, was known for manufacturing textiles, such as socks and nighties, which it supplied to retailers.Patel was a fixture in the Sunday Times Rich List with his wealth in 2006 estimated to be £105m. He was also investing heavily in property across the city and beyond.In 2007, his teenage son bought a minority stake in Preston North End Football Club. There was even a plan to build a £100m, 19-storey tower block - complete with botanical gardens and restaurant - in the centre of the city.Behind the facade, though, something very different was going on.In the early 2000s, organised crime groups had turned to large-scale attacks on the tax system through what became known as carousel fraud.Chains of fake business transactions are created as a way of stealing VAT repayments from HMRC. Goods move between different companies, into and out of the country, to generate false tax refunds.The same shipments of goods are often moved around repeatedly, hence the name carousel fraud.This type of fraud was costing taxpayers billions of pounds a year and experts like Stone were at the vanguard of the fightback.This is how Patel's textiles empire appeared on his radar."When we started to look at them we did notice some very strange shipments of goods - a container load of hats to Switzerland seemed odd because they were actually Swiss hats," he said.Image source, HMRCImage caption, The fake clothes the gang were selling would have been worth up to £50m had they have been genuineMost carousel fraudsters dealt in high-value, high-volume items like mobile phones or computer chips, for which investigators were on the lookout.But Patel's enterprise had predominantly been dealing in textiles, making the scam harder to spot.The team of investigators discovered Patel had successfully stolen more than £33m of taxpayers' money before HMRC cottoned on to what he was doing.In total, he tried to steal more than £90m of public money - the rest of the payments were stopped.Teams of investigators spent years working through vast chains of transactions until they were ready to make their move.Patel was charged with a range of offences including conspiracies to cheat the taxman, money-laundering, false accounting and selling counterfeit goods.But when he appeared at Bolton Crown Court in 2011, Patel asked the judge for permission to travel to Dubai on bail.The judge agreed to this request and Patel left the UK, never to return.In Dubai, he joined his brothers Munaf and Faisal, who had already left the country before they could be charged for their part in the conspiracy.Over the next three years, 24 members of Patel's gang were convicted. Collectively, they were jailed for more than 116 years.Image source, HMRCImage caption, A judge ordered Patel's Ferrari Superamerica to be auctioned off Efforts to have Arif Patel extradited back to the UK failed and he remained a free man in Dubai.The BBC has heard claims he had been actively seeking to strike a deal with the UK authorities to settle the case against him."In my opinion, he thought he was above justice," said Graham Honey, another former HMRC investigator. In 2020, he was working in the private sector when he said he was approached by Patel's representatives.Honey said he was asked to open up a channel of communication with HMRC and the Crown Prosecution Service because Patel wanted to make a deal.It soon became clear, however, that there would be a sticking point."It started to become apparent to me that Patel was not willing to come back," said Honey."He just thought he could get an agreement, pay some money, and this would all go away."Honey claimed that while Patel was willing to admit his guilt and repay money, he was not prepared to face a criminal trial or the prospect of time behind bars.He claimed it was not the first time that Patel had attempted to strike such a deal.Honey said: "One of the officers told me that he had said 'I'm a tiger, not a caged tiger' meaning he was a big man, he'd done what he'd done, but in essence, he wasn't prepared to go to prison for it."Image source, HMRCImage caption, HMRC said it had seized more than £78m of the gang's UK assetsIn 2023, Patel's trial got under way without him, something which is highly unusual and only done as a last resort.He was found guilty of leading one of the UK's biggest carousel fraud gangs and received a 20-year jail sentence.In 2025, he was subjected to a confiscation order to repay £90.5m through the sale of assets found to have been gained through criminality. The funds raised were to be returned to the public purse.But more than a year later, none of the money has been recouped because, despite being on the run overseas, Patel has been able to go to the Court of Appeal to object to the confiscation order.That matter has yet to be resolved.So where is Patel now and what might he have done with his stolen millions?The BBC has discovered that over the last few years, an increasing number of websites, press releases and social videos have begun to appear, celebrating the achievements of a businessman called Arif Patel in Dubai.This Arif Patel is variously a business owner, an investor and a philanthropist. The photographs on the sites are often stock images or, in at least one case, belong to a different British entrepreneur.Many of the pages also suggest Patel has links to Preston and worked in the textile industry.'Pillar of integrity' The coincidences do not end there.A story was published in 2024 in which Arif Patel denies allegations of fraud by HMRC.The article quotes a "Sam Mackenzie", who it said was a close associate of Patel.Mackenzie spoke out in support of Patel, whom he described as a "pillar of integrity".The piece also said he had received backing from an "Andrew Fox", who the article described as having reviewed the claims and deemed them to be "unfounded".It just so happens that the deputy chief constable of Lancashire police is called Sam Mackenzie, while Andrew Fox is a senior prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service.Both men had been quoted in the media following Patel's conviction.Their names appeared in other stories too, including one which claimed Patel had made a sizeable investment in HMRC anti-fraud technology in Lancashire.The BBC does not know for certain whether Patel is connected to these sites, but File on 4 Investigates has established some sites are linked to an online reputation management company based in Dubai.Another story was published earlier this year, this time about a donation Patel had made to a charitable organisation which supports children with disabilities in Dubai.It shared similarities with some of the other websites but had one key difference - it featured a genuine photograph of Patel.'Should be punished'With an up-to-date picture, facial recognition technology uncovered numerous other pictures of Patel posing at glamorous events in Dubai.We showed everything we had learned about the case to the prime minister's anti-corruption champion Dame Margaret Hodge."I think this is a shocking story of somebody who deliberately acted fraudulently and laundered money and he should be punished," she said."He should not be beyond the reach of the British justice system."I think he is clearly abusing the justice system in a way that only rich people can."There's an intrinsic injustice in a system that allows those with money to delay the implementation of a punishment for a crime and to delay the confiscation of assets which was stolen as part of that crime."The BBC contacted the Government of Dubai but did not receive a response. The BBC also contacted Arif Patel via his Manchester-based solicitor - as well as his brothers Munaf and Faisal - but did not hear back.You can listen to the File on 4 Investigates at 20:00 GMT on Tuesday 27 October.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Lancashire

title: Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
description: Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the s
body: Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite internet network.Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it. This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back".Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored."This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday.Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield. Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues.Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.Zelensky said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.Meanwhile, fighting on the ground continues.Russia's ministry of defence wrote on Telegram on Saturday that their air defences shot down 616 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones, striking a number of regions across the country, including Russian-annexed Crimea.Sergey Aksyonov, the region's Moscow-backed governor, said restrictions on electricity and water had been put in place because of power cuts caused by the drone strike.Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities said they struck a missile component manufacturer, a chemical plant and an aircraft at a military airfield inside Russia in the past 24 hours.They also said that Russia carried out 88 air strikes using 309 glide bombs and 10,270 kamikaze drones on Friday.

schema.headline: Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits

title: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams
description: Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailer
body: Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailers that claim to be family-owned firms selling quality UK-made products. Images may show a UK High Street with Union Jack flags in shot.If you order you're likely to find a product either never arrives, or is a cheap, mass-produced item from a country such as China, trading standards officers say. AI-generated images like this, as well as voice cloning and deepfake videos are increasingly being used to trick people out of their money, according to National Trading Standards.For the first time, it has drawn up an AI scam watchlist, external highlighting some of the tools and techniques criminals are using.

schema.headline: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams

body: Depending on the contract you have, data charges may apply for accessing the internet on your mobile device.If you are not sure about the potential charges, please ask your mobile network provider. You may find some costs are included in your existing price plan or that you can opt for a data package that gives reduced charges for accessing the internet.The BBC does not charge you to access mobile content.
